blocks: In nineteen twenty-two, a dying teenager in Toronto became the first person ever treated with insulin. Here's what it actually does.
After you eat, sugar from your food enters your blood. Beta cells in your pancreas sense it and release insulin.
Insulin is a key. It docks on receptors on your muscle and fat cells, and sends a message inside: open the doors.
The cell pulls sugar transporters up to its surface, and sugar flows in, out of your blood.
In type one diabetes, the immune system destroys those beta cells. No key, so sugar piles up in the blood.
Before insulin, that was a death sentence. Leonard Thompson's doctors injected a purified extract of animal pancreas, and his blood sugar came down.
Insulin has to be injected, because it's a protein. Your stomach would digest it like food.
Since nineteen eighty-two, human insulin has been made by microbes carrying the human gene.
Dosing is delicate. Too much can push blood sugar dangerously low, so it's always managed with a doctor.
